sections.text: Arjuna asked: My Lord! Those who do acts of sacrifice, not according to the scriptures but nevertheless with implicit faith, what is their condition? Is it one of Purity, of Passion or of Ignorance?
Lord Shri Krishna replied: Man has an inherent faith in one or another of the Qualities -Purity, Passion and Ignorance. Now listen.
The faith of every man conforms to his nature. By nature he is full of faith. He is in fact what his faith makes him.

So we had been discussing the Bhagavad Gita, starting from chapter one, Arjuna Vishada Yoga. The Gita opens with Dhritarashtra. Dhritarashtra, as we have discussed, is our state of mind.
Right now we live in the Dhritarashtra state. We are blind to our reality, the supreme reality, the real reality. We are blind to the truth that I am part of that supreme being, and instead we live in the world of Mamakaha -- I and mine.
So thats basically how the Bhagavad Gita started: this is our problem. All our problems start with that one misunderstanding that I am this limited being, that Mamakaha is my world, I and mine is my world. And then I separate the rest of the world as something other than me.
The next few verses focus on Duryodhana -- the Duryodhana in us. This Duryodhana represents the thief in us -- the part that wants to take away something which belongs to somebody else and make it mine. I want it so badly that I will use any means to get it.
All over our day-to-day life we see inequality in our society, because obviously there is wealth which is common to all, given by God, natural. Yet somebody hoards so much and doesnt leave enough for the others. So the Duryodhana in us wants this thing so badly.
He knows its not his, but he wants it. And therefore he is always very anxious, because he has decided: I need to have it. I know it is not mine, but I need to have it for my own happiness, to make myself complete.
This sense of incompleteness started with our state of Dhritarashtra. Because we are blind to our reality, we make ourselves limited to this self, and that I-and-mine creates incompleteness. That incompleteness has created a thief in us -- I want to take away from others and make it mine so that I will feel complete.
Thats what Duryodhana felt all his life: I need all this kingdom for myself. He was already given half the kingdom after the first match of chess, and now he wants all of it. So his mental state is that of any thief who is trying to steal something away from somebody else.
One, he is insecure -- when you are trying to steal something, you wonder: is somebody watching me? So there is insecurity, and then fear. Obviously you are fearful, you are insecure. Thats why you want to make sure you get what you want by any means.
So there are three things in that mentality: I want this so badly that Ill be willing to do anything; Im insecure; and Im fearful. The next few verses we have seen are just describing this. The first six verses said: Look at the Pandavas army -- it looks pretty well protected.
Great warriors on their side. He is basically going to Drona and saying, these are all your Shishyas. Arjun, son of Drupada, Drishtadharamna, who is now commanding the army.
So Im not sure that we are totally protected having somebody like Drona with us, because his shishyas are on the other side. Thats a fear in him. So he describes all that he feels are the weak points from looking at the other side.
And now he realizes that he may have gone overboard. When somebody is in that state, he wants to cover both bases. On one side he feels insecure.
On the other side he feels very powerful -- I have all the shrewdness and smartness and strength to do it. So first he looked at his insecurity and his weaknesses, seeing the other side as powerful. Now hes looking at it differently: no, no, I can do it.
So from verse 7 onwards, he now looks at his strength. Asmakamtu Visishtaye Tani Bauda Dwijottama. Obviously hes addressing Drona, and he said Dvijottama.
We have discussed before: Dwijottama, Dwija, Brahmin. Brahmin is considered twice born. One is a physical birth, and the second is a birth in this knowledge of who you are, which starts at the time of Upanayam when the Guru gives a mantra in his ear.
Then he goes to the Gurukul to get that education and becomes established in this knowledge. Thats why its called Dwij -- because the first is just a physical birth for a limited being, and the second birth is where he takes birth as a wise person. So therefore they are called Dwijaha.
Drona, being a Brahmin, is Dwijaha. But he said Dwijottama -- you are the best among the Brahmins. Now this could have been the best compliment in a normal situation.
But in this situation it is not because we know or at least the society knew at the time. Brahmins are soft hearted. They are not fighting type.
They are not war mongerers. They are not the ones who can be in the situation. They want to avoid this type of conflict.
We have seen that thats how Karna was caught by Parasuram. Karna went to Parasuram because he realized that other than Drona, Parasuram could teach him what the other Pandavas were learning. Parasuram had taken a vow that he would not teach any Kshatriya, because he wanted to eliminate Kshatriyas from this planet.
He would not teach this art of warfare to any Kshatriya. So Karna goes there as a Dvija, as a Brahmin. He disguises himself as a Brahmin -- lies that he is a Brahmin.
And then obviously he was a good student. One day, the teacher was sleeping with his head in Karnas lap. A bumblebee comes and sits on Karnas thigh.
He realizes that if he moves, his Guru will be disturbed, and he does not want to make his Guru uncomfortable at all. The Guru is in a deep sleep. This bumblebee bores through his flesh and blood is oozing out of that wound.
He tolerates all that pain but does not move a muscle, so that his Guru wont be disturbed in his sleep. The blood comes running down his thigh, under the Gurus head. The Guru wakes up because of the warm blood he feels.
He sees whats happening, realizes what has occurred, and Karna says, Im fine. But the Guru was angry. He said: you lied to me.
You are not a Brahmin. A Brahmin would not have been capable of tolerating this kind of pain. You are a Kshatriya who lied to me.
And then obviously, as the story goes, Karna asked for forgiveness and all of that. But Parasuram said: you will have this knowledge, but it will not come handy to you when you really need it in the battlefield. You will lose this knowledge.
The relevance here is that Dvija is not a positive compliment when you are in a war. So Duryodhana reminds Drona: look, I know you are a great teacher and a great archer and a great warrior, but in the end you are a Dvija -- so dont be soft-hearted here. Its actually his fear that maybe this guy will go soft-hearted and will not fight this battle.
Sangartam tan bravi mi te -- therefore I am going to now describe to you who are the great warriors on our side. Dont go soft-hearted on me. We have also great people on our side.
You dont need to worry about it. You just do your job. Bhavan Bismast Chakranastha starting with you Bhavan, you who are on our side so that we feel that we are protected.
Bhavan, you Bisma, Karna, Krupastha, Samitin, Jaya and Krupacharya who are victorious. All these people have good track record of resume of winning battle. Asvathama, Vikranscha, Somadatt, Tatha, Evacharya and then all others like Asvathrama.
Last time we have seen Kurupacharya is Dronacharyas brother in law and Aswathrama is Dronacharyas son. So or we cant have in one family all this bravery and valor. So hes obviously making it up a little more than what he should be.
But whatever it is, these are all great warriors. Swathama was more like Duryodhana. He was Duryodhanas best friend and was basically looking for this: if he stays with Duryodhana and Duryodhana wins the war, then he will have a kingdom of his own.
Drona and Drupada were friends and they probably learned together at some Gurus place. Drona goes to Drupada asking for some favor to make him a Raja somewhere, and Drupada insults him. Thats where their animosity started.
So the long story all weaved into it. But in the end basically Duryodhana said these are all people, the great people on our side and not only the main characters but Anyeche, Baha, Bahasuraha, Madharte, Tyakta, Jeevitaha and there are many others on our side who are ready to give up their life for me. Many, many brave people are on our side.
In other words, theyre committed to fight this war. Yudwijotama, Im not sure about you but Im sure about everybody else. They are committed to fight.
So lets do the right thing here. Nana Sastra Praharanaha, Sarve, Yuddha, Visharadaha. Not only they are ready to fight for me but they are equipped with various types of weapons.
So we are well equipped. We have a human capital, we have technology. So lets not worry about it.
Yudda Visaradaha they are expert in warfare. This verse obviously confuses everybody -- why Apar Yaptam, insufficient? Now every translation I have seen does say insufficient, even though it seems that unlimited is more appropriate here. I had asked once:, all this translation, where does that come from? And we dont get involved in this because you need a Sanskrit pandit to translate this.
He says there are Sanskrit pandits in Kashi who have translated the Bhagavad Gita after thorough discussion, and thats the translation we use. So even well-known translations do not really come from individual teachers -- they actually came from Pandits who decided on the translation. So we have to take it as it is and say Apar Yaptam in our vernacular languages.
Apariyapta is insufficient. Hes saying its insufficient. Now remember, his mentality is that of a thief.
He always feels that he is incomplete. No matter how much that person has, he will always feel there is something more he should have. And therefore his vision about what we have is never that we are sufficient.
We have plenty, so why even be fighting this battle? But even the army he sees as insufficient. All these people who went on Pandavas side -- they actually should have been on my side, and then it would have been much better. And my army is protected by Bheeshma, because he knew that Bheeshma has taken a vow that as long as he lives, he will guard the throne of Hastinapur.
Whoever is in Hastinapur, he will be protecting him. He also knows that Bheeshma has Ichamrityu -- he will only die if he wants to die. As long as Bheeshma is alive, he is protected.
So on one hand, he knows that as long as Bheeshma is on his side, he obviously does not have to worry. But at the same token he thinks: if I had more, then I would have felt a little better about it. So he said: Apariyaptam Tadasnakam Balam Vishna Bhirakshitam -- our strength protected by Bhishma still feels a little insufficient.
Whereas on the other side, Pariyaptam twidam Etesham Balam Bhima Bhirakshitam -- they are protected by Bhima. And then last time, Sid or somebody pointed out that this is not correct. Bhima was not the commander; the commander was changing every day in this army.
If you read the Mahabharata -- and I have never read it, so Im not an authority on this.

These opening verses reveal a profound truth: As is the faith, so is the person (yo yacchraddhaḥ sa eva saḥ). Krishna teaches that our faith is not merely what we intellectually believe, but the deep orientation of our entire being - it arises from our svabhava, our inherent nature shaped by past experiences and tendencies. This faith, whether sattvic, rajasic, or tamasic, colors everything we perceive and pursue. When Arjuna asks about those who worship with faith but set aside scriptural guidance, Krishna does not condemn them. Instead, he reveals that faith itself is the defining factor of who we become.
Take time today to honestly examine: What do you truly have faith in? Not what you think you should believe, but what actually drives your decisions when no one is watching. When faced with a difficult choice, what conviction do you fall back on? Consider keeping a faith journal this week - note the moments when your deepest convictions reveal themselves, whether in moments of stress, temptation, or quiet reflection. Ask yourself: Does my faith lead me toward light and clarity (sattva), toward restless ambition (rajas), or toward confusion and inertia (tamas)? Remember, awareness of our current state is the first step toward transformation.
